Key Findings

OKO holds more evidence, and richer data, than most companies at its stage.
An independent randomized trial, a peer-reviewed study, an ESSA Tier 3 certificate, and a transcript of every student utterance. These assets position OKO to build impact measurement infrastructure that advances its strategy.
Three priorities to build impact measurement infrastructure.
Decide what to measure for each element of the theory of change; build those measures into routine implementation reporting; then relate how much and how students use OKO to their growth within each district. Together they give OKO repeatable local evidence to sit alongside causal evidence.
The next causal study is a feasibility decision for OKO.
A spring 2027 quasi-experimental study makes sense only if OKO can set a prescriptive implementation model, find a credible comparison group, and fix a well-powered design in time. A second underpowered null could cost more than it gains, and time is short to set a spring QED up for success.

About OKO

OKO Labs makes Let's Talk, a supplemental math product for grades 4–10. Small groups of students work through problems with an AI facilitator that transcribes and scores their discussion. Teachers receive a report after each session. Schools and districts buy it; teachers set it up and run it. This assessment covers Let's Talk math and the measurement OKO can run on its own data. The recommendations in this assessment are intended to complement, not be redundant with, OKO's Overdeck-funded work to develop new communication and critical-thinking scores.

Theory of Change

The figure below maps how Let's Talk is intended to produce impact: from how teachers set up and run sessions through what happens in each session, what students do and what changes in them to math achievement, discussion beyond OKO and smaller gaps, within the context of small-group rotations alongside core math. Solid boxes mark elements that data or direct observation show are happening. Dashed boxes mark elements OKO describes but has not yet shown with data, including well-defined elements that are not yet measured. Numbered markers point to the open questions listed beneath the figure.

Model Description

ElementDescription
ContextStudents rarely talk to each other about math; one teacher cannot facilitate five groups at once; high-status students tend to talk most. Let's Talk is used alongside core math curricula such as Illustrative Mathematics and Eureka, in small-group rotations, in schools in several states. Schools and districts buy it; teachers run it.
Teacher setupTeachers receive onboarding and professional development on why collaboration matters and how to coach it, set up groups of two to five, and choose the math standard and session length (10–30 minutes).
In each sessionStudents solve alone, then must agree as a team; if the group splits, one wrong option is removed. After every question, the group receives a 1–4 Collaboration score with feedback about how to improve. The AI coach nudges quiet students to take part.
What students doStudents talk math with each other: explaining why, building on and correcting ideas.
What changes in studentsOKO's math discourse improves and students come to see collaboration as a skill they can build, and stronger math identity and confidence.
OutcomesOutcomes include math achievement, discussion that carries beyond OKO into regular class, and smaller achievement gaps.
Teacher report and classroom reinforcementA report reaches the teacher five minutes after each session, with scores, Top Quotes, proficiency and a next step.

Evidence Landscape

Before identifying measurement opportunities, it is worth cataloging the evidence OKO already has. This inventory is what lets the measurement priorities read as gap-filling rather than as starting from zero.

Evidence AssetWhat It ShowsLimitations
Randomized pilot trial, spring 2026SourceWestEd, independent evaluation report (August 2026)
 Twenty grade 4–5 teachers in 11 Hamilton County, Tennessee schools were randomized (1,040 students), with low attrition. Students whom teachers chose to use OKO grew more than control students (+0.31 SD above MAP projection). Collaboration scores rose 0.03 a week, and all six teachers interviewed used Top Quotes. Overall effects not significant (spring MAP g = 0.074; growth above projection g = 0.183). User comparison is not causal, because teachers chose the users. One semester only. Collaboration did not predict MAP. Control teachers rated student engagement and collaboration higher than OKO teachers did. Survey effects were smaller for economically disadvantaged students.
ESSA Tier 3 certificateSourceLXD Research, as reported by OKO (November 2026)
 OKO's evidence, as we understand it, appears consistent with the ESSA Tier 3 (promising evidence) standard. The certificate will appear on the EdTech Index. Buyers who require Tier 1 or 2 will look for a causal study with a significant overall effect.
Fractions pre-post studySourceLee, Feng and Miller, peer-reviewed CSCL 2025 paper (WestEd analysis)
 Fractions scores rose 7% after two to three weeks of use (299 students, grades 4–5), with larger gains in grade 4; math anxiety fell slightly. No comparison group; short exposure; grade 5 gains not significant.
Math Narrative Project field testSourceOKO report (January 2026) and results deck (April 2026)
 In one class, students' belief that effort fixes errors rose; questions rose to about 0.4 a minute by December; and more sessions reached Level 2 on OKO's rubric. One class of 15 students; no significance tests; the rubric was revised during the test.
Session dataSourceOKO product (Metrics List, October 2026)
 Every session yields a transcript, quote-level evidence tags, 1–4 team and student scores, solo-answer accuracy, Standards for Mathematical Practice and misconceptions, student surveys and teacher reports. Not yet linked to math outcomes. The collaboration score blends collaboration and math discourse, and is being redefined.
Implementation tracker and usage reportingSourceOKO partner success team; monthly usage summaries
 Onboarding and support milestones, usage bands by school, teachers' usage and academic goals, and monthly usage by district and school, refreshed daily. Other elements of OKO's mechanism of action / theory of change are unmeasured.

OKO's evidence is strongest inside the session: every interaction is captured, and an independent trial saw students talking math in ways rarely seen in control classrooms. Gaps include the links between session behavior and implementation quality and between either and math growth. OKO's Overdeck-funded work will strengthen the interpretability and utility of OKO-derived student scores. The priorities below target measurement that we believe current resources do not yet cover.

Cobalt also reviewed the published research behind each element of the model. That review is summarized in the appendix at the end of this report.

Impact Measurement Opportunities

Based on our review of OKO’s current capabilities and engagements with other funders and research partners, we have identified three impact measurement opportunities that correspond to the information needs of key stakeholders. Opportunity 1 maps what OKO measures against each element of the theory of change, and identifies other elements of the ToC that are not yet measured. Opportunity 2 builds those measures into an implementation reporting infrastructure. Opportunity 3 involves building OKO’s capacity to use implementation measurement to evaluate the correlation between OKO usage and student outcomes.

The Three Priorities

Measurement Focus Which audience each priority serves OKO team District leaders Teachers Funders
● Primary driver    ○ Contributing factor    – Not applicable
1 Map measurement to the theory of change Start now ● ○ ○ ○ ▼
START NOW

For each element of the theory of change, this priority involves identifying what OKO measures today, what is unmeasured but worth measuring, and candidate supplemental measures. The result is a measurement map the team can use to decide what to build. Most elements can be derived from data OKO already captures; if appropriate, the map also identifies a simple in-app student or teacher measure.

Examples of what to measure

  • Behavioral counts for the session elements: each student's share of talk, solo-answer accuracy, whether answers change after group discussion and whether they change to the right answer, and questions asked.
  • Whether the coach's nudges draw in quiet students as designed.
  • Teacher-observed collaboration outside OKO, using OKO's own standard: unprompted, specific anecdotes count; prompted agreement does not.
  • For each element, the team's hypothesis about whether it predicts math growth, to be tested in Priority 3.
2 Make the active ingredients visible Next 2–4 months ● ● ○ – ▼
BUILD NEXT

This priority involves building a reporting system to summarize measures identified and/or developed in priority 1 with reports designed to meet the needs of the OKO team and district partners at the classroom, school and district level. The goal is that report viewers can see, for any classroom, whether Let's Talk is being used as designed.

What to measure (illustrative only)

  • Whether solo-then-agree runs as designed in each session.
  • How talk is spread within each group, and participation by student subgroup, as a check that quieter and lower-status students are included.
  • Dose by student, against the recommended 30 minutes a week.
  • Teacher report opens, followed by regrouping or re-teaching.
3 Relate use to growth End of 2026–27 school year ● ● – ● ▼
ANALYZE

This priority involves developing the internal capacity to routinize correlational analyses quantifying the relationship between OKO implementation–particularly the measures derived in priority 1 and reported in Priority 2—and student outcomes. Repeated each year in each district, it answers the question superintendents ask after hearing about a study somewhere else: will it work with my students?

The first step is deciding on what student outcomes to measure. These could include growth in collaboration and related scores derived from OKO's AI, self- or teacher-reported durable skills, measures of math competence, and district diagnostics (e.g. MAP or i-Ready).

What to do

  • Clarify what outcomes to measure and the process for measuring them.
  • Build pipes to link outcome data to OKO implementation data (from priorities 1 and 2).
  • Determine the correlational analysis to be run.
  • Build/automate correlational analyses into reporting platform.
  • Include capability of examining results by student subgroup.

What Changes If You Do This

Today OKO can show that students talk math in its sessions and that their scores rise, and it has one trial with mixed results. With these three priorities in place, OKO could tell a district, in spring, how its own classrooms used Let's Talk: whether students solved alone before agreeing, whether quiet students took part, and how much the students whose teachers used it well grew compared with classmates who used it less. It could see which session ingredients go with math growth and which do not, and adjust the product accordingly. And it could design its next causal study with implementation measures that more meaningfully relate to the elements of OKO that are designed to produce positive student outcomes.

Recommended Next Steps

The priorities translate into a short list of near-term actions. Most are OKO's to take; where Cobalt could help, we say so.

Immediate

1
Work through the theory of change together. TJ, Lauren and Cobalt walk through the model element by element: what OKO measures, what it does not, and which three or four elements the team would bet predict math growth.
2
Confirm the Overdeck scope. OKO confirms which measurement work the Overdeck grant covers, so the priorities complement it rather than duplicate it.
3
Settle the growth measure. OKO decides the design of its pre/post tests and identifies at least one district willing to share MAP or i-Ready data.
4
Evaluate whether a spring QED is feasible. This is OKO's decision and OKO's work. A quasi-experimental study makes sense only if a prescriptive implementation model is feasible, a credible comparison group exists, and the design, including a power analysis, is fixed before the winter benchmark window. It is not yet clear what sample would be adequately powered.

After immediate steps

5
Scope Priorities 2 and 3. Agree owners, costs and the division of labor, including what Cobalt supports.
6
Run the first within-district analysis. Apply Priority 3 at the end of the 2026–27 school year in the districts with a growth measure in place.
7
Revisit a full-year RCT. Decide on a 2027–28 trial once the implementation measures exist to build into its design.

About This Report

This report has two purposes: first, building on and reflecting OKO’s logic model and other source materials, to describe the mechanisms through which Let's Talk is intended to produce impact; and second, to identify where measurement would most improve OKO's ability to understand and demonstrate that impact.

Our aim is to describe a path for OKO to build the capacity to measure, report, and use the elements of Let's Talk sessions that most directly reflect its “active ingredients”, and the capacity to routinely link that information with student math growth and other key outcomes.

Where sources disagree on study results, we rely on WestEd's independent report; on how the product works, we rely on OKO's own documents.
